To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

genetic risk for multiple sclerosis is primarily due to variants within the MHC, that the MHC class I region exerts a protective effect, and that variation within non-MHC immunological loci, particularly those related to T cell differentiation, also contribute to susceptibility.

the genetic risk of multiple sclerosis is determined by a large number of loci of which the MHC exerts the greatest influence, that the majority of these loci have a role in regulating the differentiation of T helper cells, and that the HLA A and HLA DRB genes are responsible for the independent effects of class I and class II genes on disease risk.
the genetic architecture of multiple sclerosis is highly complex with at least 30 susceptibility loci, most of which have a small effect on risk.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the identification of genetic factors contributing to multiple sclerosis.
the identification of the genetic factors that influence the development of multiple sclerosis.
the genetic basis of multiple sclerosis and we have made significant contributions to the field.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
the genetic architecture of multiple sclerosis is complex and involves at least 30 loci in all.
the disease is caused by a complex interplay between the environment, immune system and genetic risk.

the genetic susceptibility of multiple sclerosis is primarily attributable to variation within the human leukocyte antigen gene complex, but that a large number of additional risk alleles are dispersed throughout the genome.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
30-40% of multiple sclerosis risk can now be explained with common genetic variants and there is no longer a need to postulate the existence of non-HLA alleles conferring a very large effect.
the genetic architecture of multiple sclerosis has complexity that includes both common and uncommon variants, where both might be associated with functional pathways in the immune system.
the most important risk factor in multiple sclerosis is genetic and the most important genes are within the major histopathology complex.
The main takeaway from our work is that
there are at least 30 loci that have been robustly associated with the disease.
multiple sclerosis is a complex genetic disease, with genetic factors accounting for about 50% of the risk for developing the disease.
there are many more genetic variants involved in multiple sclerosis susceptibility than previously thought.
